items.name: Wari-Bateshwar and the first towns
items.description: At Wari-Bateshwar, on the old Brahmaputra in Narsingdi, archaeologists have found a fortified town with ramparts and a moat, a paved road, punch-marked silver coins, rouletted ware and beads of semi-precious stone, dated from about the 5th century BCE. It was probably a river port trading with the Mediterranean and Southeast Asia, and some scholars identify it with Sounagoura, named by Ptolemy. Greek and Latin writers describe a powerful people of the Ganges delta, the Gangaridai, whose war elephants were said to have deterred Alexander in 326 BCE.

items.name: Pundranagara and the Mauryas
items.description: Mahasthangarh, on the Karatoya river near Bogra, was Pundranagara, capital of the Pundra country (Pundravardhana) and the oldest city site in Bangladesh. A limestone plaque in Brahmi script found there, of the Mauryan period (3rd century BCE), records a governor’s order to relieve famine with grain and coins from the city storehouse. The walled citadel was occupied for some 1,500 years, through the Shunga, Kushan, Gupta and Pala periods. Vanga (the south and east of the delta) and Pundra appear in the Mahabharata and the Jain and Buddhist texts.

items.name: Gupta Bengal and Samatata
items.description: Samudragupta’s Allahabad pillar (c. 350) lists Samatata, the south-eastern delta, as a frontier kingdom paying tribute, while Pundravardhana in the north became a Gupta province (bhukti) whose copper-plate land grants, from Damodarpur and Baigram, are among the earliest dated documents of Bengal. After the Guptas weakened in the 6th century, independent kings ruled Vanga from the east (the Faridpur grants of Gopachandra, Dharmaditya and Samacharadeva), striking gold coins.

items.name: Shashanka and the Gauda kingdom
items.description: Shashanka, king of Gauda from about 590, ruled from Karnasuvarna (near Murshidabad) the first great independent kingdom of Bengal, reaching into Bihar and Odisha. He killed Rajyavardhana of Thanesar (606), which set him against Harsha, and Buddhist writers such as Xuanzang accused him of persecuting Buddhists. His era is used in the Bengali calendar tradition, and after his death (c. 637) Bengal fell into a century of disorder the texts call matsyanyaya, the law of the fishes.

items.name: Samatata and the Khadga kings
items.description: In the 7th century the Khadga dynasty, Buddhist kings, ruled Samatata (around Comilla) and Vanga. The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang visited Samatata about 639 and counted some thirty monasteries and two thousand monks; Sengzhi found the Khadga king Rajabhata a devout patron. At Mainamati, the hills west of Comilla, the Shalban Vihara and other monasteries were built by the later Deva kings of the 8th century.

items.name: The Pala Empire
items.description: Around 750 the chiefs of Bengal chose Gopala as king to end the matsyanyaya, founding the Pala dynasty, which ruled Bengal and Bihar for four centuries. Dharmapala (c. 775–812) and Devapala (c. 812–850) fought the Pratiharas and Rashtrakutas for Kannauj, and the Palas were the greatest patrons of Mahayana and Vajrayana Buddhism, founding the universities of Vikramashila and Somapura. Mahipala I (c. 988) restored the empire after decline; Rajendra Chola raided Bengal (c. 1021); and the Kaivarta revolt in Varendra (c. 1075) was put down by Ramapala before the Senas took over.

items.name: Somapura Mahavihara and the Buddhist universities
items.description: Dharmapala founded the Somapura Mahavihara at Paharpur, in Naogaon district, in the late 8th century: a monastery of 177 cells round a vast cruciform temple, one of the largest south of the Himalayas and now a World Heritage Site. With Vikramashila and Nalanda in Bihar and the monasteries of Mainamati, it made Bengal a centre of Buddhist learning; the scholar Atisha Dipankara, born at Vikrampur (c. 982), taught there before carrying Buddhism to Tibet in 1042. The Charyapada songs, the earliest Bengali poetry, come from these Buddhist circles.

items.name: The Chandra dynasty of Vanga
items.description: The Chandra kings, Buddhists from Harikela, ruled south-east Bengal (Samatata, Vanga and Srihatta) from Vikrampur, near Dhaka, in the 10th and 11th centuries. Shrichandra (c. 930–975) was the greatest; his copper plates grant land in Sylhet and the Mainamati hills, and the dynasty struck silver coins. Rajendra Chola’s armies reached Vanga about 1021, and the Chandras gave way to the Varmans in the mid-11th century.

items.name: The Varmans and the Senas
items.description: The Varmans, a Hindu dynasty from Kalinga, ruled Vanga from Vikrampur in the late 11th century. The Senas, Brahmin-warriors from Karnataka settled in Rarh, rose as Pala vassals; Vijayasena (c. 1096–1159) took Vikrampur from the Varmans and Gauda and Varendra from the Palas, uniting Bengal. Ballalasena and Lakshmanasena patronised Sanskrit poetry (Jayadeva’s Gita Govinda) and Brahmanical reform. Bakhtiyar Khalji surprised Lakshmanasena at Nadia about 1204, and the later Senas held on in Vikrampur for a few decades.

items.name: Bakhtiyar Khalji and Lakhnauti
items.description: About 1204 the Turkic general Muhammad Bakhtiyar Khalji, having sacked the Buddhist monasteries of Bihar, rode into Nadia and drove out Lakshmanasena, founding a Muslim state at Lakhnauti (Gaur). His successors, the Khalji maliks and then governors sent from Delhi, often rebelled; Balban crushed Tughral Khan in 1281 and left his son Bughra Khan, whose line ruled almost independently. Sufi saints such as Shah Jalal, who came to Sylhet in 1303, spread Islam in the east. Ghiyath al-Din Tughluq divided Bengal into three provinces (Lakhnauti, Satgaon and Sonargaon) in 1324.

periods.name: Bakhtiyar Khalji and the Khalji maliks
The Balbani house and the three provinces

items.name: The Deva kings and the south-east
items.description: In the 13th century, while Muslim rulers held Lakhnauti, Hindu kings of the Deva dynasty ruled Samatata, Chittagong and later Vikrampur: Damodaradeva’s copper plate of 1243 grants land near Chittagong, and Dasharathadeva took Vikrampur from the last Senas. The south-east was taken into the Bengal sultanate only in the early 14th century.

items.name: The Bengal Sultanate
items.description: Fakhruddin Mubarak Shah declared himself independent at Sonargaon in 1338, and Shamsuddin Ilyas Shah united Bengal in 1352, beating off two Delhi invasions; the land became known as Bangalah. Under the Ilyas Shahi, Ganesha and Hussain Shahi dynasties the sultans ruled from Pandua and Gaur, minted silver tankas, traded with Ming China (Zheng He’s fleet called in 1405 and 1421) and built brick mosques such as the Adina Mosque (1373) and the Choto Sona Mosque. Alauddin Husain Shah (1494–1519) patronised Bengali literature, and Chaitanya’s Vaishnava movement flourished. Sher Shah Suri took Gaur in 1538.

periods.name: Ilyas Shah and the union of Bengal
The Habshi and Hussain Shahi sultans

items.name: Khan Jahan Ali and Bagerhat
items.description: Khan Jahan Ali, a Sufi general, cleared the Sundarbans forest edge in the mid-15th century and founded the mosque city of Khalifatabad at Bagerhat, with roads, tanks and some fifty brick buildings; its Sixty Dome Mosque (Shat Gambuj) is the largest medieval mosque in Bangladesh, and the city is a World Heritage Site. He died in 1459 and his tomb is a place of pilgrimage.

items.name: Arakan, the Portuguese and Chittagong
items.description: Chittagong, the delta’s great port, was fought over by the sultans of Bengal, the kings of Tripura and the kingdom of Mrauk U in Arakan, which held it for most of the period from about 1459 to 1666. Portuguese traders settled there and at Hooghly from the 1530s, and Portuguese and Arakanese raiders (the Magh) carried off thousands from the delta to the slave markets. Arakan’s court patronised Bengali poets such as Alaol. The Mughal governor Shaista Khan took Chittagong in 1666 and renamed it Islamabad.

periods.name: The Portuguese and the Magh raiders

items.name: Cooch Behar and Tripura
items.description: On Bengal’s northern and eastern edges stood Hindu kingdoms. Biswa Singha founded the Koch kingdom about 1515; under Nara Narayan and his general Chilarai it dominated the north-east, then split (1581), and Cooch Behar lost Rangpur to the Mughals in 1687 and accepted East India Company protection in 1773. The Manikya kings of Tripura (Twipra) ruled the hills east of Comilla, at times holding the plains and Chittagong, and became Mughal vassals; both survived as princely states until 1949.

items.name: Sher Shah, the Karranis and the Mughal conquest
items.description: Sher Shah Suri took Gaur from the last Hussain Shahi sultan (1538) and, after beating Humayun, ruled Bengal from Delhi; the Grand Trunk Road ran from Sonargaon to the Indus. After the Surs, the Afghan Karrani sultans ruled Bengal and Odisha from Tanda (1564–1576). Akbar’s generals beat Daud Khan Karrani at Tukaroi (1575) and killed him at Rajmahal (1576), and Bengal became a Mughal province, though the east held out for decades.

items.name: Isa Khan and the Baro-Bhuiyans
items.description: In the river country of the east, the Bhati, the twelve chiefs (Baro-Bhuiyans) led by Isa Khan of Sonargaon and Katrabo resisted the Mughals with fleets of war boats; Isa Khan beat the Mughal admiral at Egarasindhur (1584) and fought Man Singh to a standstill (1597). His son Musa Khan was defeated by Islam Khan Chishti, who made Dhaka the Mughal capital in 1610 and broke the Bhuiyans by 1611.

items.name: Mughal Bengal and Jahangirnagar
items.description: Bengal was the richest province of the Mughal Empire. Islam Khan moved the capital to Dhaka, named Jahangirnagar (1610); its muslin, silk and saltpetre drew Dutch, English and French traders, and the subahdars built the Bara Katra (1644) and the Lalbagh Fort. Shaista Khan (governor 1664–1688) took Chittagong from Arakan (1666) and made rice so cheap in Dhaka that his rule was remembered for it. The Mughal revenue reforms spread rice farming east into the delta, where Islam became the majority faith.

items.name: The Nawabs of Bengal
items.description: Murshid Quli Khan, the Mughal revenue minister, became the first Nawab of Bengal in 1717 and moved the capital to Murshidabad. The nawabs ruled Bengal, Bihar and Odisha in practice independently, paying tribute to Delhi. Alivardi Khan (1740–1756) fought off a decade of Maratha raids (the Bargis, 1741–1751) at the cost of Odisha. His grandson Siraj ud-Daulah took Calcutta from the English in 1756.

items.name: Plassey, Buxar and the Company’s diwani
items.description: Robert Clive defeated Siraj ud-Daulah at Plassey on 23 June 1757 with the help of the nawab’s general Mir Jafar, whom the East India Company made nawab. After the Battle of Buxar (1764) the Mughal emperor granted the Company the diwani, the right to collect Bengal’s revenue (1765). Ruthless collection during the drought of 1769–1770 helped turn it into the Great Bengal Famine, in which perhaps a third of the people died. Warren Hastings made Calcutta the capital of British India (1772), and Cornwallis’s Permanent Settlement (1793) fixed the land tax with the zamindars.

items.name: Company Bengal: peasants and reformers
items.description: Under Company rule the eastern districts grew jute and indigo for export while the zamindars of the Permanent Settlement drew rent. Haji Shariatullah’s Faraizi movement (from 1818) and Titumir’s rising (1831) rallied Muslim peasants against landlords and indigo planters; the Sepoy Mutiny of 1857 broke out among troops at Barrackpore and Dhaka. In Calcutta, the Bengal Renaissance of Ram Mohan Roy and the Hindu College remade Bengali prose and education.

items.name: British Bengal and the 1905 partition
items.description: After 1858 Bengal was ruled by the Crown. Lord Curzon partitioned the province in 1905, creating Eastern Bengal and Assam with Dhaka as its capital; Hindu protests (the Swadeshi movement) led to its reversal in 1911, while Muslim leaders founded the All-India Muslim League at Dhaka in 1906. Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in 1913, and A. K. Fazlul Huq’s Krishak Praja Party spoke for the peasants. The Bengal famine of 1943 killed some three million people.

items.name: Partition and East Pakistan
items.description: At the partition of India in August 1947 the Muslim-majority eastern half of Bengal, with Sylhet by referendum, became East Bengal, renamed East Pakistan in 1955. Separated from West Pakistan by 1,600 km of India, it had the majority of Pakistan’s people but little of its power or investment. The United Front swept the 1954 provincial election, and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman’s Six Points (1966) demanded autonomy; the Agartala conspiracy case against him fuelled the 1969 mass uprising.

items.name: The Language Movement
items.description: When Pakistan’s leaders declared Urdu the sole state language, students in Dhaka demanded equal status for Bengali. On 21 February 1952 police fired on a student demonstration at Dhaka University, killing several; the Shaheed Minar marks the spot, and 21 February is now International Mother Language Day. Bengali was recognised as a state language in the 1956 constitution.

items.name: The Liberation War
items.description: After the Awami League won the 1970 election, the Pakistani army began Operation Searchlight in Dhaka on the night of 25 March 1971; independence was declared on 26 March. During nine months of war the Mukti Bahini fought the army and its militias, who killed hundreds of thousands of civilians in what is widely recognised as a genocide, and about ten million refugees fled to India. India entered the war on 3 December, and Pakistani forces surrendered in Dhaka on 16 December 1971, Victory Day.

items.name: Mujib, coups and military rule
items.description: Sheikh Mujibur Rahman returned in January 1972 as founding leader; the 1972 constitution set out nationalism, socialism, democracy and secularism. Famine (1974) and one-party rule under BAKSAL were followed by Mujib’s assassination with most of his family on 15 August 1975. General Ziaur Rahman took power (1977) and founded the BNP before his own assassination (1981), and General Hussain Muhammad Ershad ruled from 1982 until a mass movement forced him out in December 1990.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Assassination of Sheikh Mujibur Rahman

items.name: Modern Bangladesh
items.description: Parliamentary democracy returned in 1991, and power alternated between Khaleda Zia’s BNP and Sheikh Hasina’s Awami League, with a military-backed caretaker government in 2007–2008. The garment industry made Bangladesh one of the world’s largest clothing exporters, and poverty fell sharply despite cyclones, floods and the Rana Plaza collapse (2013); the country has sheltered about a million Rohingya refugees since 2017. Hasina ruled from 2009 until a student-led uprising forced her to flee in August 2024; Muhammad Yunus heads an interim government.
